passage.text:
Cycle routes notice
The cycle routes team needs helpers on Saturday. Bring gloves and arrive before nine.

Message from a friend
I have booked the safe paths session for Tuesday, but I may arrive late. Please start without me and save a place.

Information sign
Visitors to the cycle routes may use the tools, but they must return them before leaving.

Short announcement
The commuters meeting has moved from Room 2 to Room 4 because the first room is being painted.

Notice for members
Members can borrow one safe paths guide for a week. Ask at the desk if you need another copy.

passage.text: The people below want to choose from cycle routes. Decide which option is most suitable.

passage.label: A
passage.text: Flat riverside beginner loop — A flat twelve kilometre loop that follows the river and is ideal for riders trying their first route. Bikes and helmets are hired at the start, the path is smooth with no hills, and groups leave every afternoon. A leader stays at the back so nobody is left behind.

passage.label: B
passage.text: Weekend off road mountain trail — A challenging off-road trail across rocky hills for experienced riders who own a mountain bike. The weekend route covers rough ground, steep climbs and river crossings, with no bicycle hire available. Riders carry their own water, food and repair tools. The start lies two hours from town, reached by an early train, so planning ahead is essential.

passage.label: C
passage.text: Family tricycle mornings — A short morning loop where tricycles and balance bikes are offered to young children who have never ridden. Parents ride free alongside, the distance is under three kilometres, and a playground stop breaks the route. Helmets and pads are included for every child, and a helper stays at the front, so sessions finish before noon.

passage.label: D
passage.text: Night city loop with lights — A ten kilometre evening loop through quiet streets, lit from start to finish with free lights and high-visibility vests. Riders sign up at the library, the ride leaves at seven and returns by ten, and there is no charge at all. The surface is smooth and even, which makes the loop suitable for commuter bikes.

passage.label: E
passage.text: Free audio guided woodland ride — A free self-guided route through the woodland with audio stories played from your phone. Riders must bring their own bicycle, there is no hire or repair service along the way, and phone signal disappears in the deepest trees. The path winds gently and takes about two hours to complete at a relaxed pace.

passage.label: F
passage.text: Race training with weekly coach — An eight week programme with a dedicated speed coach, aimed at riders preparing for a local race. Sessions run on weekday mornings, include timed laps and video feedback, and finish with entry to the race itself. Riders must already ride regularly. The cost covers coaching and a race number, but riders supply their own bicycles.

passage.label: G
passage.text: Scenic coast ride with support van — A scenic forty kilometre coastal ride with a support van that carries bags and collects anyone who tires early. A lunch stop is included at a village café, and the ride follows the cliff road with wide sea views. Riders should have done a long ride before.

passage.label: H
passage.text: Budget route on your own bike — A free weekday route where riders bring their own bicycle and receive no equipment or support. The path is flat and easy, but evenings are crowded with commuters, and there is no lighting after dark. It suits riders who simply want a quick ride after work on their own bicycles.

questions.prompt: Liam has never cycled on a road and owns no bike. He wants a flat, safe path with hired equipment, has one free afternoon, and needs a leader close by in case he struggles.
Priya owns a mountain bike and rides every weekend. She wants a difficult off-road route with steep climbs and no bike hire needed, and she is willing to catch an early train to reach the start.
Oliver rides with his five-year-old daughter, who has never ridden a bike. He wants a short morning ride, child-sized cycles, a safe surface and a rest stop with play equipment.
Fatima works until six every evening and cannot pay extra fees. She wants a free ride after dark, with lights supplied, on quiet streets, returning home by ten.
Daniel is training for his first race and wants to get faster. He is free on weekday mornings, would value a coach and timed practice, and already cycles twice a week.

passage.text: When the commuters in our town started a cycle routes project, few residents expected it to grow so quickly. At first, the organisers met in a small room and planned one simple activity involving safe paths. They soon discovered that people were more willing to join when they could see a clear benefit for the neighbourhood. The organisers therefore published a short timetable and invited local businesses to offer practical help.

The project was not completely easy. Some volunteers were worried that the work would take too much time, while others wanted to change the plan every week. The team solved this by giving each person one small responsibility and reviewing the results together. This made the project feel manageable, and it also meant that new volunteers could contribute without special experience.

Looking back, the organiser says the most important lesson was not the final result but the way people learned to cooperate. The group still has problems, especially when the weather affects outdoor work, yet members now discuss solutions rather than blaming one another. For this reason, the project has become a useful example of how a modest local idea can create lasting connections.

parts.passageTitle: Part 4 – The Commuters' Route Plan Takes Shape

passage.text: Every morning, office workers walked from the station to the business park along a narrow pavement. A commuter named Elena counted how many crossed through an unofficial gap in the fence instead of using the distant crossing. She shared the numbers online, and forty people replied. (16) ..... She summarised their comments and invited everyone to discuss possible routes at the station café.

The group mapped three routes that avoided the busiest junction. They measured each one with a phone app and recorded cracked pavement or poor lighting. Elena compiled the findings into a short report and sent it to the local transport office. (17) ..... Two group members later presented the same detailed findings at a public council session.

The transport office replied within a month, saying one route could be improved with a crossing and better signs. The group was surprised by the quick response. A council officer explained that evidence from the phone app had strengthened their case. (18) ..... The commuters celebrated the news by walking the chosen route together on a sunny afternoon.

Construction of the new crossing began in September and took six weeks. Meanwhile, the group organised walking buddies so nobody had to use the dark gap alone. Commuters who had never spoken before began meeting at the station entrance each morning. (19) ..... One regular walker said those conversations made the six-week delay pass far more quickly than expected.

When the crossing opened, Elena found that almost nobody used the fence gap. The business park added a coffee cart, and the council planted two trees beside the path. The group continued meeting monthly to check safety. (20) ..... The coffee seller served forty customers on the first morning, which made the improved route feel welcoming as well as safer. Elena kept her original report to show other residents how careful observations could support a practical request.

passage.text: The walking buddy system turned a frustrating delay into a chance to build friendships.

passage.label: B
passage.text: Elena said the trees were a small touch that made the whole route feel finished.

passage.label: C

parts.passageTitle: Part 5 – Riders Meet and Share Ideas

passage.text: The commuters usually meet (21) ........ Saturday. New members are shown how to (22) ........ the equipment. They can ask for advice if they are (23) ........ about a task. The group works together (24) ........ everyone can learn. Members often share ideas (25) ........ the session. The project has become a popular way to meet (26) ........ people. During the trial, riders were asked to record anything that made the route confusing or uncomfortable. The group then met to compare their notes and suggest practical improvements. Some members wanted clearer signs, while others asked for better lighting. The organisers considered each idea before sending a summary to the council. The trial also showed that good communication was important. A short online map explained the safer sections, and signs warned riders where construction was taking place. At the next meeting, the group reviewed the comments and agreed which changes should be requested first.

parts.passageTitle: Part 6 – Safe Riding Along the Paths

passage.text: The commuters meet (27) ........ week to plan activities. New members learn (28) ........ to use the safe paths safely. They can join the work, (29) ........ they should follow the group’s instructions. The project has kept useful materials (30) ........ being thrown away. It is a place (31) ........ people can exchange ideas. Remember (32) ........ ask for help when you need it. The cycling group continues to meet because conditions on the roads change throughout the year. Members share information about repairs, weather and busy junctions, and they remind new riders to use lights after dark. Their regular discussions have made more people confident about choosing a bicycle for short journeys. The project has not solved every problem, but it has given residents a clearer voice. By collecting information carefully and discussing it openly, the cyclists can suggest improvements that benefit people using different kinds of transport.
